usage: Warmer and more heartfelt than 아주; common when talking about people or feelings
Adds emotional weight; sounds sincere, not exaggerated
Works for weather/states; slightly more expressive than 너무
무척이나 adds extra emphasis and a literary, emotional tone
examples: 오늘 회식 무척 즐거웠어요.
Today's company dinner was really enjoyable.
Good for thanking a boss or coworker sincerely
한국 음식이 무척 입에 맞아요.
Korean food really suits my taste.
입에 맞다 = to suit one's palate, a natural set phrase
그 소식을 듣고 무척 놀랐어요.
I was really surprised to hear that news.
Pairs naturally with emotion verbs like 놀라다, 기뻐하다
nuance: 무척 means 'very' but carries a warm, emotional flavor, so it fits feelings, people, and personal reactions more than dry facts. Koreans often choose it over 아주 when they want to sound sincere rather than clinical. In very casual texting people lean on 너무 or 진짜 instead, but 무척 sounds nicely heartfelt in speech.
mistakes: Using 무척 with a negative like 'not very' — for that you want 그다지 안 / 별로 안, not 무척 안.
Treating it as slang; 무척 is fully standard and slightly soft/literary, so it never sounds rude or too casual.

usage: Very common everyday intensifier, stronger than 아주
Often used for size, amount, or impressiveness
Expresses genuine surprise at a high degree
The adjective 굉장하다 stands alone: 우와, 굉장하다! = Wow, amazing!
examples: 이 카페 디저트가 굉장히 인기가 많아요.
This cafe's desserts are incredibly popular.
인기가 많다 = to be popular, a fixed phrase
면접 준비를 굉장히 열심히 했어요.
I prepared incredibly hard for the interview.
Pairs well with 열심히 to stress effort
오늘 지하철이 굉장히 붐비네요.
The subway is extremely crowded today.
붐비다 = to be crowded; natural commuter complaint
nuance: 굉장히 is one of the most reachable strong intensifiers in everyday Korean and sounds natural in both casual and polite speech. It leans toward describing impressiveness, scale, or intensity, so it shines with adjectives like 크다, 많다, 맛있다. It is a notch stronger and more vivid than 아주, but still completely standard for work emails and conversation.
mistakes: Writing 굉장이 — the correct spelling is 굉장히 with 히.
Overusing it on tiny things; saying 굉장히 for a minor matter can sound like exaggeration, where 꽤 or 좀 would fit better.

usage: Sounds measured and slightly formal; common in reviews
Polished tone, good for feedback and work talk
Adnominal 상당한: 상당한 시간 = a considerable amount of time
examples: 이번 프로젝트가 상당히 까다로웠어요.
This project was considerably tricky.
Sounds professional in a work debrief
그 동네는 월세가 상당히 높은 편이에요.
Rents in that neighborhood are considerably high.
-은 편이다 = tends to be, softens the claim
설명이 상당히 자세해서 도움이 됐어요.
The explanation was quite detailed, so it helped.
Common when giving polite positive feedback
nuance: 상당히 means a notable, measured degree and carries a slightly formal, composed tone, so it fits reviews, reports, and adult conversation well. Compared with the more emotional 무척 or casual 되게, it sounds objective and a bit understated, as if you are reporting a fact. It is a favorite in written feedback and workplace speech where you want to sound thoughtful.
mistakes: Using it in very casual chat with friends, where it can sound stiff — 되게 or 엄청 are more natural there.
Confusing the adverb 상당히 with the adnominal 상당한; you need 상당한 directly before a noun (상당한 노력), not 상당히.

usage: You're pretty good (better than I expected)
Notes that something has reached a real degree
Standalone praise: 오, 제법인데? = Oh, not bad!
examples: 한국어 실력이 제법 늘었네요.
Your Korean has improved quite a bit.
Warm compliment with a hint of pleasant surprise
아침저녁으로 제법 쌀쌀해졌어요.
It's gotten fairly chilly morning and evening.
쌀쌀하다 = chilly; classic autumn small talk
이 식당, 가격은 싼데 맛은 제법이에요.
This place is cheap but the food is actually quite good.
Shows the nuance of exceeding expectations
nuance: 제법 means 'fairly' but with the special nuance that something turned out better or more than you expected, often with a touch of admiration. Telling someone 제법 잘하네요 is a compliment, while a flat 잘하네요 is more neutral. Because it implies surprise, avoid it about things you always expected to be good — there it can sound faintly condescending.
mistakes: Using 제법 toward a clearly skilled senior or expert, where the 'surprisingly good' nuance can feel patronizing.
Treating it as a plain synonym for 아주; 제법 specifically signals 'more than expected,' not just a high degree.

usage: Formal, softening tone for notices and emails
Diplomatic way to express mild disappointment
examples: 배송이 다소 지연되어 죄송합니다.
We apologize that the delivery is somewhat delayed.
Standard wording in shop and delivery messages
오늘은 어제보다 기온이 다소 낮겠습니다.
Today the temperature will be somewhat lower than yesterday.
Weather-forecast register; you hear this on TV
설명이 다소 복잡하니 천천히 읽어 주세요.
The explanation is rather complex, so please read it slowly.
Polite hedge in instructions
nuance: 다소 means 'somewhat / a little' but belongs to formal written and broadcast Korean, so you see it in notices, weather reports, and customer messages rather than chat with friends. It softens a statement politely, much like English 'somewhat,' and pairs often with mildly negative words (지연, 부족, 아쉽다). In casual speech Koreans say 좀 or 약간 instead, so reserve 다소 for polished contexts.
mistakes: Using 다소 in casual conversation with friends, where it sounds oddly stiff — use 좀 instead.
Pairing it with very strong words; 다소 implies a small-to-moderate degree, so 다소 엄청 is contradictory.

usage: Very common for taste, temperature, feelings
Cooking instruction: just briefly in hot water
Please open the door just a bit
Softens an emotion in a cute, casual way
examples: 국이 살짝 싱거운데 소금 좀 넣을게요.
The soup is slightly bland, so I'll add some salt.
싱겁다 = bland; everyday kitchen talk
오늘 컨디션이 살짝 안 좋아요.
I feel slightly off today.
Casual, friendly way to mention feeling unwell
가격이 살짝 부담되긴 해요.
The price is a touch burdensome, honestly.
살짝 softens the complaint and sounds natural
nuance: 살짝 means 'slightly' but with a light, gentle, often cute feeling, used for small actions, mild tastes, and softened emotions. It is extremely common in casual speech and cooking, where it suggests doing something briefly or to a small degree. Compared with the neutral 약간, 살짝 feels more vivid and conversational, almost like 'just a touch.'
mistakes: Using 살짝 for large or serious degrees; it only describes small, light amounts.
Forgetting it also modifies actions (살짝 만지다 = touch lightly), not just adjectives — it is not purely a 'somewhat' word.

usage: Must pair with a negative; stresses total inability
I just can't understand it at all
이해가 안 가다 = it doesn't make sense to me
It just won't work no matter what
잠이 안 오다 = sleep won't come
examples: 이 서류가 도무지 무슨 말인지 모르겠어요.
I simply can't tell what this document is even saying.
Great for venting about confusing paperwork
요즘 일이 많아서 도무지 시간이 안 나요.
I'm so busy lately that I just can't find any time.
시간이 나다 = to have time free
몇 번을 봐도 도무지 답을 모르겠어요.
No matter how many times I look, I just can't get the answer.
몇 번을 봐도 = however many times I look
nuance: 도무지 means 'not at all / simply (cannot)' and must be used with a negative, expressing total impossibility plus a feeling of frustration. It is close to 도저히 but leans slightly more toward 'I cannot grasp/understand,' often about confusion. Because it demands negation, it never appears in positive sentences — 도무지 좋아요 is impossible.
mistakes: Using 도무지 in a positive sentence; it only works with negation (안, 못, 모르다, -지 않다).
Confusing it with 도대체 (what on earth); 도대체 questions, while 도무지 emphasizes inability.

usage: Almost always used with comparisons; often before 더
Stresses a big gap between two things
버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 = much faster than the bus
나아요 = better; common when comparing conditions
examples: 지하철이 택시보다 훨씬 빨라요.
The subway is much faster than a taxi.
Classic A보다 B 훨씬 comparison structure
약 먹고 나니까 훨씬 괜찮아졌어요.
After taking the medicine, I feel much better.
괜찮아지다 = to get better; comparing before/after
이 집이 전에 살던 곳보다 훨씬 넓어요.
This place is far more spacious than where I lived before.
Natural when comparing apartments
nuance: 훨씬 is the go-to word for emphasizing a large gap in comparisons, equivalent to 'much/far more.' It pairs naturally with 더 and with the 보다 comparative structure, and it implies the difference is significant, not slight. Unlike plain intensifiers, 훨씬 almost always needs something to compare against, even if that comparison is just implied by context.
mistakes: Using 훨씬 with no comparison at all; saying 훨씬 좋아요 out of nowhere sounds incomplete — there must be an implied 'than X.'
Replacing 아주/너무 with 훨씬 for a simple high degree; 훨씬 is specifically comparative, not a general 'very.'

usage: Super common in casual speech, like spoken 'really'
Everyday complaint about distance or effort
Mainly spoken; in writing people prefer 정말/아주
examples: 여기 분위기 되게 좋다, 자주 오자.
This place has a really nice vibe, let's come often.
분위기 = vibe/atmosphere; casual 반말 here
그 영화 되게 재밌었어요, 추천해요.
That movie was so fun, I recommend it.
Natural casual recommendation
오늘 길이 되게 막히네요.
The roads are really jammed today.
막히다 = to be congested; everyday gripe
nuance: 되게 is a very common casual intensifier meaning 'really/so,' almost exclusively used in spoken Korean among friends and peers. It feels lively and natural in conversation but looks out of place in formal writing or business emails, where 아주 or 정말 fit better. Younger people use it constantly, so recognizing 되게 is key to following everyday speech.
mistakes: Writing 되게 in formal documents or emails, where it sounds too casual — use 정말/아주 instead.
Spelling it 됬게 or 돼게; the correct form is 되게.

usage: Strong, casual; great for amounts and intensity
Common spoken intensifier among all ages
Adjective form: 효과가 엄청나요 = the effect is huge
examples: 주말이라 마트에 사람이 엄청 많아요.
It's the weekend so the mart is super crowded.
Everyday observation, very natural
이번 시험 공부를 엄청 했는데 떨려요.
I studied a ton for this exam but I'm nervous.
떨리다 = to feel nervous/shaky
배달이 엄청 빨리 왔어요.
The delivery came incredibly fast.
Pairs with 빨리; common food-delivery comment
nuance: 엄청 is a punchy, casual way to say 'super / a ton,' stressing a large amount or high intensity. It is slightly more colloquial than 굉장히 and is extremely frequent in everyday speech and texting. It works for quantity (엄청 많다) and intensity (엄청 덥다) alike, and the related 엄청나다 lets you use it as a full adjective.
mistakes: Using 엄청 in formal writing where it reads as too casual; choose 매우/대단히 there.
Saying 엄청 with tiny degrees; like other strong intensifiers it implies a genuinely large amount, not 'a little.'

usage: Often paired with 더; implies stepping up a level
Common in product or service descriptions
Formal-ish, used for improvement and progress
examples: 앱을 업데이트하니까 한층 더 편해졌어요.
After updating the app, it became even more convenient.
Natural when reviewing an app or service
연습을 꾸준히 했더니 실력이 한층 늘었어요.
Since I practiced steadily, my skills improved even further.
한층 stresses a clear step up
가을이 되니 단풍이 한층 아름다워요.
Now that it's autumn, the foliage is even more beautiful.
단풍 = autumn leaves; slightly literary tone
nuance: 한층 means 'even more / a level higher,' picturing improvement as climbing one more step from an already-good state. It is a bit more polished and written-sounding than 더, so it fits reviews, descriptions, and thoughtful speech. It almost always implies a positive upgrade and frequently appears as 한층 더 for extra emphasis.
mistakes: Using 한층 for a first-time degree with no prior baseline; it implies going 'one level further' from an existing state.
Treating it as fully casual; in chatty 반말 a simple 더 or 훨씬 usually sounds more natural.

usage: Implies a sudden, visible rise over a short time
Notes a marked change in someone's appearance
부쩍 자주 보이네요 = I see you around a lot more lately
examples: 요즘 부쩍 피곤해서 일찍 자요.
I've been noticeably more tired lately, so I sleep early.
요즘 + 부쩍 is a very natural pairing
환절기라 그런지 감기 환자가 부쩍 늘었어요.
Maybe because of the season change, cold patients have increased markedly.
환절기 = change of seasons
조카가 못 본 사이에 부쩍 컸어요.
My niece/nephew has grown so much since I last saw them.
못 본 사이에 = while I wasn't seeing them
nuance: 부쩍 describes a marked, noticeable change that happened over a relatively short period, often 'suddenly a lot more.' It pairs most naturally with verbs of change like 늘다, 줄다, 커지다, 추워지다, and with 요즘 to mean 'lately, noticeably.' Unlike steady-change words such as 점점, 부쩍 stresses that the jump is striking and easy to notice.
mistakes: Using 부쩍 with static adjectives (부쩍 예쁘다 sounds odd); it wants verbs of change like 예뻐졌다.
Confusing it with the gradual 점점/차츰; 부쩍 implies a sharp, noticeable jump, not slow change.
